**Surah 31 (Luqman), verses 1–11: Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan)**

Meccan. It has 2,110 letters, 548 words, and 34 verses.

Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn al-Qasim ibn Ahmad al-Faqih informed me, saying: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mu'addal informed me, saying: Abu Yahya al-Bazzar informed me, from Muhammad ibn Mansur, from Muhammad ibn Imran ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, who said: my father related to me, from Mukhalad ibn 'Abd al-Wahid, from al-Hajjaj ibn 'Abd Allah, from Abu al-Khalil, from 'Ali ibn Zayd and 'Ata' ibn Abi Maymuna, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surah Luqman, Luqman will be his companion on the Day of Resurrection, and he will be given ten good deeds for each act of kindness he performed, and for each wrong he committed." [[Tafsir Nur al-Thaqalayn: 4/193, no. 2; Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 8/74.]]

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Alif, Lam, Mim. These are the verses of the Wise Book. A guidance and a mercy for the good-doers. Those who establish the prayer, give the zakat, and are certain of the Hereafter: those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful.

[The reading of] the common (Qur'anic) readers is with the accusative (naṣb) of *hudan wa-raḥmatan* as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) and as an accusative of separation (qaṭ'), while Hamza read *wa-raḥmatun* with the nominative (raf') as a nominal inception (ibtida').

His saying: "And among people is one who purchases idle talk (lahw al-ḥadith)..."

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith ibn 'Alqama ibn Kalada ibn 'Abd al-Dar ibn Qusayy. He used to trade, going out to Persia, buying the tales of the non-Arabs, narrating them and telling them to the Quraysh, saying: "Muhammad tells you the story of 'Ad and Thamud, and I tell you the story of Rustam and Isfandiyar and the reports of the non-Arabs and the Kings (Akasira)." They would find his talk pleasing and abandon listening to the Qur'an. Mujahid said: It means buying the singing-girls (qiyan) and the singers. The grammatical structure under this interpretation is: "he purchases a female (dhāt) or a [thing] of idle talk (dhā lahw al-ḥadith)."

Abu Tahir Muhammad ibn al-Fadl ibn Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Muzakki informed us in the year 383, saying: My grandfather Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Khuzayma related to me, from 'Ali ibn Khuzayma, from 'Ali ibn Hujr, from Mustamghal ibn Mulajjan al-Ta'i, from Mutarrah ibn Yazid, from 'Ubayd Allah ibn Zajr, from 'Ali ibn Yazid, from al-Qasim, from Abu Umama, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It is not lawful to teach singing-girls, nor to sell them, and their price is forbidden. In the like of this was this verse revealed: 'And among people is one who purchases idle talk, to mislead from the way of Allah...'"

[180] [[Sunan al-Tirmidhi: 2/375, with variation; al-Sunan al-Kubra: 6/14; Kanz al-'Ummal: 4/39.]] to the end of the verse.

And no man raises his voice in singing except that Allah sends upon him two devils, one on this shoulder and the other on that shoulder, and they keep striking him with their feet until he is the one who falls silent.

Others said: The meaning is that he substitutes and chooses idle talk, singing, flutes, and instruments over the Qur'an. And [they interpreted] "the way of Allah" as the Qur'an.

Abu al-Sahba' al-Bakri said: I asked Ibn Mas'ud about this verse, and he said: "It is singing, by Allah, there is no god but Him," repeating it three times. Similarly Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Jurayj said: It is the drum. 'Ubayd related from al-Dahhak: It is shirk. Juwaybir related from him: It is singing, and he said: "Singing corrupts wealth, provokes the Lord's anger, and corrupts the heart." Thawir ibn Abi Fakhita related from his father from Ibn 'Abbas: This verse was revealed concerning a man who bought a slave-girl who sang to him night and day. Everything of speech that diverts from the way of Allah toward what He has forbidden is idle talk, and singing is among it, and other things besides it. Qatada said: It is every idle talk and play. 'Ata' said: It is trivialities and nonsense.

Makhul said: Whoever buys a singing slave-girl (*ḍarraba*) to keep her for her singing, and remains persistent in this until he dies, I will not pray over him. Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: "And among people is one who purchases idle talk..." to the end of the verse.

'Ali ibn Yazid related from al-Qasim ibn Abi Umama, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, the Exalted, sent me as a mercy and a guidance to the worlds, and commanded me to obliterate musical instruments, flutes, strings, the cross, and the affairs of the Jahiliyya. My Lord swore by His might: no servant of Mine will drink a sip of wine deliberately except that I will give him to drink of pus equal to it on the Day of Resurrection, whether he is forgiven or punished. And no one will give it to a young child, weak and Muslim, except that I will give him to drink of its equal of pus on the Day of Resurrection, whether he is forgiven or punished. And whoever abandons it out of fear of Me, I will give him to drink from the pools of holiness on the Day of Resurrection. Their sale is not lawful, nor their purchase, nor their teaching, nor trade in them, and their price is forbidden." [181] [[Musnad Ahmad: 5/268.]]

He means the beaters (*ḍawārib*, i.e., the tambourine players). Hammad related from Ibrahim, who said: Singing causes hypocrisy to grow in the heart. And our companions used to take hold of the mouths of the alleys and burn the tambourines.

'Abd Allah ibn Hamid informed us, from Ibn Shadhan, from Jaghwayh, from Salih ibn Muhammad, from Ibrahim ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, who said: It has reached me that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says on the Day of Resurrection: "Where are those who used to keep themselves and their ears pure from idle talk and the flutes of Satan?" Admit them into the gardens of musk. Then He says to the angels: "Let My servants hear My praise, My laudation, and My glorification," and inform them that "no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve."

His saying: "to mislead from the way of Allah without knowledge, and take it in mockery." Al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, and Ya'qub read *wa-yattakhidha-ha* with the fatha on the dhal, coordinating it with his saying "to mislead," and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd, who said: "because of its proximity to the accusative." The others read it with the nominative (raf') coordinating it with his saying "purchases."

For them is a humiliating punishment. And when Our verses are recited to him, he turns away arrogantly, as if he did not hear them, as if there were deafness in his ears. So give him the good news of a painful punishment. Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them are gardens of bliss, abiding therein; the promise of Allah is true, and He is the Mighty, the Wise. He created the heavens without pillars that you see, and cast into the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you, and dispersed therein every kind of creature, and We sent down water from the sky and caused to grow therein every noble pair (*zawjin karimin*), i.e., a good kind. This which you have mentioned, which they witness, is the creation of Allah. So show me what those besides Him created, [meaning] your gods which you worship. Rather, the wrongdoers are in manifest error.

Then He says to the angels: "Let My servants hear My praise, My laudation, and My glorification," and inform them that "no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve."

His saying: "to mislead from the way of Allah without knowledge, and take it in mockery." Al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, and Ya'qub read *wa-yattakhidha-ha* with the fatha on the dhal, coordinating it with his saying "to mislead," and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd, who said: "because of its proximity to the accusative." The others read it with the nominative (raf') coordinating it with his saying "purchases."

For them is a humiliating punishment. And when Our verses are recited to him, he turns away arrogantly, as if he did not hear them, as if there were deafness in his ears. So give him the good news of a painful punishment. Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them are gardens of bliss, abiding therein; the promise of Allah is true, and He is the Mighty, the Wise. He created the heavens without pillars that you see, and cast into the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you, and dispersed therein every kind of creature, and We sent down water from the sky and caused to grow therein every noble pair (*zawjin karimin*), i.e., a good kind. This which you have mentioned, which they witness, is the creation of Allah. So show me what those besides Him created, [meaning] your gods which you worship. Rather, the wrongdoers are in manifest error.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 31, verses 12–21 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾. It means reason, knowledge, acting upon it, and correctness in matters.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Yasar said: He was Luqman ibn Ba'ur ibn Bahur ibn Tarikh, and Tarikh is Azar. Wahb said: He was the son of Ayyub's sister. Muqatil said: It is mentioned that Luqman was the son of Ayyub's maternal aunt.

Al-Waqidi said: He was a judge among the Children of Israel. The scholars agreed that he was wise, but that he was not a prophet, except 'Ikrimah, who said: Luqman was a prophet. He stood alone in this view.

Abu Mansur al-Jamshadhi narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Yusuf narrated to me, from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from 'Abd Allah ibn Hashim, from Waki', from Isra'il, from Jabir, from 'Ikrimah, who said: Luqman was a prophet. Some of them said: Luqman was given the choice between prophethood and wisdom, and he chose wisdom.

'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar narrated, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Truly I say, Luqman was not a prophet, but he was a servant of Allah, abundant in reflection, good in certainty [in the source: "al-zann", opinion], who loved Allah, so Allah loved him, and He granted him wisdom by guarantee." [182] [Kanz al-'Ummal: 14/34.]

[It is narrated that at the beginning of his affair] Luqman was sleeping at midday when a call came to him: "O Luqman, would you like Allah to make you a khalifah (vicegerent) on earth, judging between people with truth?" He answered the voice, saying: "If my Lord gives me the choice, I will accept well-being and not accept trial. If He resolves upon me, then I hear and obey. For I know that if He does that to me, He will protect me and help me." The angels then said, in a voice they did not show, "Why, O Luqman?" He said: "Because the judge is in the most difficult and turbid of positions; injustice overtakes him from every place. If he is saved, it is well; and if he errs, he has erred from the path to Paradise. He who is humbled in this world [and honored in the Hereafter] is better than he who is honored in this world [and humbled in the Hereafter]."

Whoever prefers this world over the Hereafter, this world will tempt him and he will not attain the Hereafter. The angels marvelled at the goodness of his speech. Then he slept a sleep, and he was given wisdom. He woke up speaking it. [al-Muhadhdhab al-Bari' of Ibn Fahd: 4/454; Tarikh Dimashq: 17/85.]

Then Dawud was called after him, and he accepted it, but he did not stipulate what Luqman stipulated, so he fell into error more than once, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, pardoned him every time. Luqman used to support him with his wisdom. Dawud said to him: "Blessed are you, O Luqman. You were given wisdom and turned away from trial. Dawud was given the caliphate and was afflicted with calamity and temptation."

Al-Imam Abu Mansur ibn al-Jamshadhi narrated to us, in wording, saying: Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Yusuf narrated to me, from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad, from 'Abd Allah ibn Hashim, from Waki', from Muhammad ibn Hassan, from Khalid al-Rab'i, who said: Luqman was an Abyssinian slave and a carpenter. Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Fanjawayh informed us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn Malik al-Qati'i narrated to me, from 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal, from his father, from Aswad ibn 'Amir, from Hammad, from 'Ali ibn Yazid, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, that Luqman was a tailor.

﴿Be grateful to Allah﴾: meaning, "We said to him: be grateful to Allah."

﴿And whoever is grateful, he is only grateful for his own soul, and whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾.

Mujahid said: Luqman was a black slave with large lips and cracked feet. al-Awza'i narrated from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Harmalah, who said: A black man came to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, asking him. Sa'id said to him: "Do not grieve because you are black, for among the best of people were three from the blacks: Bilal, Mihja' the freedman of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and Luqman the wise. Luqman was a black Nubian from the blacks of Egypt, with thick lips."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when Luqman said to his son — his name was An'am — while he was advising him: "O my son, do not associate anything with Allah. Indeed, association is a great injustice."﴾ ﴿And We have enjoined upon man [regarding] his parents. His mother carried him, in weakness upon weakness﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: hardship upon hardship. al-Dahhak: weakness upon weakness. Qatadah: exertion upon exertion. Mujahid and Ibn Kaysan: difficulty upon difficulty.

﴿And his weaning is in two years﴾: its weaning, i.e. his removal from breastfeeding. It is narrated from Ya'qub: "wa-fisaluhu" (and his weaning).

﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents; to Me is the destination﴾. 'Abd Allah ibn Hamid al-Isfahani informed us, from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Balkhi, who said: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Balkhi informed me, from Nasir ibn Yahya, from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, concerning the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: "Give thanks to Me and to your parents." He said: Whoever prays the five prayers has given thanks to Allah, and whoever supplicates for his parents after the prayers has given thanks to his parents.

﴿And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them, but accompany them in this world with kindness﴾: good companionship; and its meaning is "with what is fair".

﴿And follow the way of those who turn back to Me﴾: take the path of Muhammad and his companions.

﴿Then to Me is your return, and I will inform you of what you used to do﴾. These two verses were revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and his mother, and the story has already passed.

﴿O my son, indeed it, if it be the weight of a mustard seed﴾. Some grammarians said: This pronoun refers to the sin and disobedience, meaning: indeed the disobedience, if it be. What supports this is the saying of Muqatil: An'am, the son of Luqman, said to his father: "O father, if I do a sin where no one sees me, how will Allah know it?" So he said to him: "O my son, indeed it, if it be..." Others said: this "ha'" is a supporting pronoun (imad), and it was made feminine because he took it to the grain, as in the saying of the poet:

"And he chokes on the word he has spread, as the spear's chest is choked with blood."

The "mithqal" may be read in the accusative or nominative: the accusative as the predicate of kana, and the nominative as its subject, and its meaning: "if there occurs" (in tam, complete usage), and then it has no predicate: ﴿then it would be in a rock﴾. Qatadah said: in a mountain. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a rock beneath the seven earths, and it is where the deeds of the wicked are recorded, and the greenness of the sky is from it. al-Suddi said: Allah created the earth upon a fish, which is the nun that Allah mentioned in the Qur'an: "Nun. By the pen" [68:1]. The fish is in the water, the water is on the back of a rock, the rock is on the back of an angel, and the angel is on a stone, and this is the rock that Luqman mentioned. It is neither in the heavens nor in the earth, and the rock is on the wind.

﴿Or in the heavens or in the earth — Allah will bring it forth. Indeed, Allah is Subtle [in extracting it], Acquainted [with its place].﴾ I saw in some books that Luqman (peace be upon him) said to his son: "O my son, indeed it, if it be the weight of a mustard seed..." to the end of the verse. He trembled from the awe of this word and died, and it was the last of his wisdom.

His saying: ﴿O my son, establish prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and bear patiently what befalls you. Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾: that is, the obligatory matters which Allah has commanded. Ibn 'Abbas said: the firm matters. Muqatil: the rightful matters.

﴿And do not turn your cheek [in contempt] toward people﴾. al-Nakha'i, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn Mahisn, Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "tusa'ir" with an alif.

Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Abu Habash informed me, Abu al-Qasim ibn al-Fadl said, Abu Zur'ah said: Nadr ibn 'Ali narrated to me, saying: my father informed me, from Mu'alla al-Warraq, from 'Asim al-Jahdari: "wa-la tusir khaddaka" with a damma on the ta' and a jazm on the sad, from "asara". The rest read "tusa'ir" from al-tasa'ir (the verb form). Ibn 'Abbas said: He means: do not be arrogant so that you belittle people and turn away from them with your face when they speak to you. Mujahid: it is the man who has a grudge between him and you, so you meet him and he turns his face away from you. 'Ikrimah: it is the one who, when greeted, twists his neck out of arrogance. al-Rabi' and Qatadah: do not belittle the poor; let the poor and the rich be equal in your sight. 'Ata': it is the one who twists his cheek.

'Abd Allah ibn Hamid informed us, from Hamid ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Salih, from 'Abd al-Samad, from Kharijah ibn Mus'ab, from al-Mughirah, from Ibrahim concerning His saying: "And do not turn your cheek toward people." He said: It is exaggerated speech (al-tashdiq fi al-kalam). al-Mu'arrikh said: do not frown at people's faces.

The origin of this word is inclination. It is said: "a man is asar" when his neck is inclined. Its plural is "sa'ar", and from it: al-sa'r, which is a disease that afflicts camels in their necks and heads until it twists their necks. The arrogant man who turns away from people in contempt for them is compared to that. A poet describing camels said:

"We brought them into the course of Suhayl, southerly, with the 'sa'r' of the desert, among the herd and the stragglers."

That is, inclined in the desert. Another said:

"And when the tyrant turned his cheek, we straightened him from his inclination, and he was made straight."

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾, meaning in conceit. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love everyone self-deluded and boastful﴾, in his walking, boasting over people.

'Abd Allah ibn Hamid al-Wazzan informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Shadhan, from Jaygawayh, from Salih ibn Muhammad, from Jarir ibn 'Abd al-Hamid, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from his father, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man went out swaggering in the Jahiliyyah, wearing a garment. So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, commanded the earth, and it seized him, and he continues sinking into it until the Day of Resurrection." [Musnad Ahmad: 2/222; Kanz al-'Ummal: 3/537, with variation in the hadith.]

﴿And be moderate in your walking﴾: be humble, and do not swagger, and let your walk be moderate, neither with conceit nor with haste.

Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn al-Husayn ibn Mihran al-Muqri' informed us in the year 381 [AH], saying: Abu al-'Abbas Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Surraj and Abu al-Wafa' al-Mu'ayyad ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Isa informed me, both saying: 'Abbas ibn Muhammad al-Duri said, from al-Walid ibn Salamah, judge of Jordan, from 'Umar ibn Sahban, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umran, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Haste in walking takes away the radiance of the believer." [183] [Kanz al-'Ummal: 15/412, no. 41620.]

﴿And lower your voice﴾, and reduce it: ﴿Indeed, the most disagreeable of voices is the voice of donkeys﴾. Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: the ugliest. Its beginning is a groan and its end is a sob; He commanded him to moderate his voice. 'Ikrimah and al-Hakam ibn 'Uyaynah said: the most intense. Ibn Zayd said: If raising the voice were good, He would not have assigned it to donkeys.

Abu Zakariyya Yahya ibn Isma'il al-Hari informed us, saying: Abu Hamid Ahmad ibn 'Abdun ibn 'Ammarah al-A'mash informed me, saying: Abu Hatim Muhammad ibn Idris al-Handhali informed me, from Yahya ibn Salih al-Wuhadhi, from Musa ibn A'yan, who said: I heard Sufyan say concerning the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: "Indeed, the most disagreeable of voices is the voice of donkeys": "The cry of every thing is glorification of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, except the donkey." It was also said: because it brays without benefit.

al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn Fanjawayh informed me, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Bishr, who said: Abu Bakr ibn Abi al-Khasib informed me, from 'Abd Allah ibn Jabir, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Walid al-Harrani, from 'Uthman ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from 'Anbasah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from Muhammad ibn Zadhan, from Umm Sa'd, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, dislikes three voices: the bray of the donkey, the bark of the dog, and the cry for war." [184]

Chapter on mention of some of the wisdom narrated from Luqman.

'Abd Allah ibn Hamid al-Wazzan al-Isfahani informed us, from Ahmad ibn Shadhan, from Jaygawayh ibn Muhammad [from Salih ibn Muhammad], from Ibrahim ibn Abi Yahya, from Muhammad ibn 'Ajlan, who said: Luqman said: "No wealth is like health, and no bounty is like a contented soul."

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Dinawari informed us, from 'Umar ibn Ahmad ibn al-Qasim al-Nahawandi, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Ghaffar al-Zarqani, from Abu Sukayn Zakariyya ibn Yahya ibn 'Umar ibn [Hafs (in the Isfahan copy: Hisn)], from his paternal uncle Abu Zajr ibn Hisn, from his grandfather Humayd ibn Minhab, who said: Tawus narrated to me, from Abu Hurayrah, who said:

A man passed by Luqman while people were gathered around him, and said: "Are you not the black slave who used to be a shepherd in such-and-such a place?" He said: "Yes." He said: "So what has brought you to what I see?" He said: "Truthfulness in speech, fulfilling trusts, and leaving what does not concern me."

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad informed me, saying: Abu al-Husayn Bakr ibn Malik al-Qati'i informed me, from 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal, from Ubayy, from Waki', who said: Abu al-Ashhab informed me, from Khalid al-Rab'i, who said: Luqman was an Abyssinian slave and a carpenter. His master said to him: "Slaughter a sheep for us." So he slaughtered a sheep for him. He said: "Bring me the best of its two morsels." So he brought him the tongue and the heart. He said: "Was there anything in it better than this?" He said: "No." He said: [Luqman] was silent about him, then said to him: "Slaughter a sheep for us," so he slaughtered a sheep, and he said: "Throw away its two worst morsels." So he threw away the tongue and the heart, and he said: "I ordered you to bring me the best of its two morsels, and you brought me the tongue and the heart; and I ordered you to throw away the worst of its two morsels, and you threw away the tongue and the heart?!" He said: "Because there is nothing better than them when they are good, and nothing worse than them when they are bad."

al-Husayn ibn Muhammad informed me, from Ahmad ibn Ja'far ibn Hamdan, from Yusuf ibn 'Abd Allah, from Musa ibn Isma'il, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Anas, that Luqman was with Dawud (peace be upon him) while he was weaving a coat of mail. Luqman kept marvelling at what he saw, and wanted to ask him, but his wisdom prevented him from asking. When he finished it, brought it and poured it out, he said: "What a fine coat of war this is!" Luqman said: "Indeed, among wise sayings is silence, and few are those who practise it."

[al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn Mahan informed me, from 'Ali ibn Muhammad al-Tanafasi (in the Isfahan copy: Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, from Ibn Shanbah, who said: 'Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Mahan narrated to us, from 'Ali ibn Muhammad al-Tanafasi)], who said: Abu Usamah and Waki' informed me, both saying: Sufyan informed us, from his father, from 'Ikrimah, who said: Luqman was among the least valued of his master's slaves. His master sent him with some slaves to an orchard of his to bring them some of its fruit. They came, having nothing with them, for they had eaten the fruit, and they blamed Luqman. Luqman said to his master: "The one of two faces is not trustworthy before Allah. Give me and them hot water to drink, then send us, and we will return." He did so, and they began to vomit that fruit, while Luqman vomited water. So his truthfulness and their lying became known.

He said: The first of his wisdom that was narrated: while he was with his master, he entered the privy and sat there a long time. Luqman called out to him: "Prolonged sitting over a need brings harm to the liver, produces hemorrhoids, and sends heat up to the head. So sit gently and rise gently." He said: So he came out and wrote his wisdom on the door of the latrine. [Tafsir al-Durr al-Manthur: 5/161, on the verse.]

He said: One day his master became drunk and bet some people that he would drink the water of a lake. When he sobered up, he realized what he had got into, so he summoned Luqman and said: "For such a thing I had chosen you." He said: "Bring out your chair and your jugs, then gather them." When they had gathered, he said: "On what did you bet?" They said: "That he would drink the water of this lake." He said: "It has sources. Block its sources from it." They said: "And how can we block its sources from it?" Luqman said: "And how can he drink it while it has sources?!"

al-Husayn ibn Muhammad informed me, from 'Ubayd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Shanbah, from 'Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Mahan, from 'Ali ibn Muhammad al-Tanafasi, who said: Abu al-Husayn al-'Ukli informed me [from 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal, from Dawud ibn 'Umar, from Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash, from 'Abd Allah ibn Dinar, that Luqman came back from a journey,] [In the Isfahan copy: from Abu al-Husayn al-'Ukli, from Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah al-Muzani, from his father, who said: Luqman said: "A father's beating of his child is like manure for the crop." al-Husayn ibn Muhammad informed me, saying: Abu Bakr ibn Malik narrated to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal narrated to us, saying: Dawud ibn 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash narrated to us, from 'Abd Allah ibn Dinar, that Luqman came back from a journey... the hadith.] and he met his servant on the road, and said: "What did my father do?" He said: "He died." He said: "Praise be to Allah, I have taken possession of my affair." He said: "What did my wife do?" He said: "She died." He said: "Renew my bedding." He said: "What did my sister do?" He said: "She died." He said: "She has covered my nakedness." He said: "What did my brother do?" He said: "He died." He said: "My back is broken."

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 31, verse 12–21 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad informed me, saying: Abu Bakr ibn Malik informed me, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal, from my father, from Sufyan, who said: It was said to Luqman: "Which of people is the most evil?" He said: "The one who does not care that people see him doing wrong." It was said to Luqman: "How ugly is your face!" He said: "Do you find fault with this on the engraving or on the engraver?"

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and has completed upon you His blessings?﴾

Nafiʿ, Shaybah, Abu Jaʿfar, Abu Raja' al-ʿUtaridi, Abu Mijlaz, Abu ʿAmr, al-Aʿraj, Ayyub and Hafs read "niʿamahu" (His blessings) in the plural with a pronoun suffix (idafah). Abu ʿUbayd, Abu Muʿadh al-Nahwi and Abu Hatim preferred this reading. The others read it in the singular with tanwin (niʿmatan), and its meaning is also plural. Its evidence is the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And if you count the blessings of Allah, you cannot enumerate them﴾ [Ibrahim: 34]. Mujahid and Sufyan said: they are "there is no god but Allah." Confirming this also is what Abu al-Qasim [al-Habibi] [sic in the original] informed me: that he saw in the codex of ʿAbd Allah "niʿmatahu" with the suffix and the singular, ﴿apparent and hidden﴾. They differed concerning it and said much.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: As for the apparent, it is religion and adornment; as for the hidden, it is what is concealed from the servants and known to Allah.

Muqatil: The apparent is the proportion of creation, provision and Islam; the hidden is the sins of the children of Adam that were concealed, so no one knew of them and they were not punished for them.

al-Dahhak: The apparent is beauty of form, height of stature and balance of limbs; the hidden is forgiveness.

al-Qurazi: The apparent is Muhammad (ﷺ), and the hidden is knowledge of Him.

Rabi': The apparent is by the limbs and the hidden is by the heart.

ʿAta' al-Khurasani: The apparent is the lightening of the laws, and the hidden is intercession.

Mujahid: The apparent is the manifestation of Islam and victory over enemies; the hidden is support with angels.

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Naysaburi informed us, saying: Abu al-Fadl Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn Mahmash informed us, saying: Abu Yahya Zakariyya ibn Yahya ibn al-Harb informed me, from Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Muhammad ibn Sabiq al-Kufi, who said: Abu Malik al-Jibni informed me, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, who said: I asked Ibn ʿAbbas about the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and has completed upon you His blessings, apparent and hidden﴾. He said: "This is from my memorized (reports) that I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what are these apparent and hidden blessings?' He said: 'As for the apparent, it is Islam, what is beautiful of your character, and what is bestowed upon you of provision. As for the hidden, it is what covers the evil of your deeds. O Ibn ʿAbbas, Allah the Exalted says: "I have made for the believer a third (of his reward) in the prayers of the believers over him after the cessation of his deeds, by which I expiate his sins; and I have made for him a third of his wealth so that he may expiate his sins by it; and I have concealed his evil deed which, if I were to reveal it to people, his family would cast him off, and others besides them."'"

Muhammad ibn ʿAli al-Tirmidhi said: The apparent blessing is ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed upon you My blessing﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], and the hidden is His saying: ﴿and I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3].

al-Harith ibn Asad al-Muhasibi [in the Isfahan copy: al-Harb ibn Asad al-Muharibi]: The apparent is the delight of this world, and the hidden is the delight of the Hereafter. ʿAmr ibn ʿUthman al-Sadafi: The apparent is the lightening of the laws, and the hidden is the multiplying of crafts.

It is said: The apparent is the reward, and the hidden is contentment. Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah: The apparent is following the Messenger, and the hidden is love for him. It is said: The apparent is the balancing of outward forms, and the hidden is the purifying of inner secrets. It is said: The apparent is clarification, its evidence being His saying: ﴿Allah makes clear to you lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisa': 176] and ﴿and He makes clear His signs to the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221]; and the hidden is adornment, as in His saying: ﴿and has made it beautiful in your hearts﴾ [al-Hujurat: 7]. It is said: The apparent is provision earned, and the hidden is provision ﴿from where he does not expect﴾.

It is said: The apparent is the entrance of food, and the hidden is the exit of harm. It is said: The apparent is the limbs, and the hidden is the interests. It is said: The apparent is creation, and the hidden is character. It is said: The apparent is bestowal of bounty, its evidence being His saying: ﴿those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7], and the hidden is teaching, as in His saying: ﴿and teaches you what you did not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 151]. It is said: The apparent is what is given and granted of blessings; it is said the hidden is what is folded and withheld of various kinds of trial. It is said: The apparent is the call, its evidence being His saying: ﴿and Allah calls to the abode of peace﴾ [Yunus: 25], and the hidden is guidance, its evidence being His saying: ﴿and guides whom He wills﴾ [Yunus: 25].

It is said: The apparent is support with angels, and the hidden is casting terror into the hearts of the disbelievers. It is said: The apparent is the detailing of acts of obedience, namely that He mentions your obedience one by one, praises you for it and rewards you for it, its evidence being His saying: ﴿the repentant﴾ [al-Tawbah: 112], and His saying: ﴿The believers have certainly succeeded﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 35] to the end of the verse. And the hidden is the summary of sins, for He called you to repentance from them by the name of faith without enumerating and detailing them, its evidence being His saying: ﴿And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you, O believers﴾ [al-Nur: 31]. It is said: The apparent is the sending down of rain and showers, and the hidden is the reviving of regions and cities.

It is said: The apparent is success in acts of worship, and the hidden is sincerity and protection from showing off. It is said: The apparent is the remembrance of the tongue, and the hidden is the remembrance of the heart. It is said: The apparent is recitation of the Qur'an, and the hidden is knowledge of it. It is said: The apparent is the light of day for activity and livelihood, and the hidden is the darkness of night for rest and repose. It is said: The apparent is speech, and the hidden is intellect. It is said: The apparent is His blessing upon you after you came out of your mother's womb, and the hidden is His blessing upon you while you were in your mother's womb.

It is said: The apparent is the manifest testimony, and the hidden is the prior happiness. It is said: The apparent is the variety of gifts, and the hidden is the forgiveness of sins. It is said: The apparent is the removal of burden and the raising of remembrance, and the hidden is the expansion of the breast.

It is said: The apparent is the opening of paths, and the hidden is the stripping of kingdoms from those who oppose You. It is said: The apparent is wealth and children, and the hidden is guidance and direction. It is said: The apparent is the sound word, and the hidden is confirmation and making upright. It is said: The apparent is what Allah expiates of sins through calamities and trials, and the hidden is what He pardons and does not hold you accountable for in this world and the Hereafter. It is said: The apparent is what lies between you and His creation of kinship and marriage ties, and the hidden is what lies between you and Him of nearness, secrets, and intimate conversation in the early hours. It is said: The apparent is height, its evidence being His saying: ﴿and you will be the superior ones﴾ [Al 'Imran: 139], and the hidden is nearness, its evidence being His saying: ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 11].

His saying: ﴿And among people is one who argues about Allah without knowledge or guidance or an illuminating Book﴾. It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith when he claimed that the angels are daughters of Allah. ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon."﴾

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Even though Satan invites them to the punishment of the Blaze?﴾ Al-Akhfash said: its wording is interrogative but its meaning is affirmative (taqrir). Abu ʿUbayda said: "law" here has an omitted answer; its implied sense is: ﴿Even though Satan invites them to the punishment of the Blaze?﴾, i.e., its requirements, so that they would follow him.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 31, verses 12–21 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾. It means reason, knowledge, acting upon it, and correctness in matters.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Yasar said: He was Luqman ibn Ba'ur ibn Bahur ibn Tarikh, and Tarikh is Azar. Wahb said: He was the son of Ayyub's sister. Muqatil said: It is mentioned that Luqman was the son of Ayyub's maternal aunt.

Al-Waqidi said: He was a judge among the Children of Israel. The scholars agreed that he was wise, but that he was not a prophet, except 'Ikrimah, who said: Luqman was a prophet. He stood alone in this view.

Abu Mansur al-Jamshadhi narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Yusuf narrated to me, from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from 'Abd Allah ibn Hashim, from Waki', from Isra'il, from Jabir, from 'Ikrimah, who said: Luqman was a prophet. Some of them said: Luqman was given the choice between prophethood and wisdom, and he chose wisdom.

'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar narrated, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Truly I say, Luqman was not a prophet, but he was a servant of Allah, abundant in reflection, good in certainty [in the source: "al-zann", opinion], who loved Allah, so Allah loved him, and He granted him wisdom by guarantee." [182] [Kanz al-'Ummal: 14/34.]

[It is narrated that at the beginning of his affair] Luqman was sleeping at midday when a call came to him: "O Luqman, would you like Allah to make you a khalifah (vicegerent) on earth, judging between people with truth?" He answered the voice, saying: "If my Lord gives me the choice, I will accept well-being and not accept trial. If He resolves upon me, then I hear and obey. For I know that if He does that to me, He will protect me and help me." The angels then said, in a voice they did not show, "Why, O Luqman?" He said: "Because the judge is in the most difficult and turbid of positions; injustice overtakes him from every place. If he is saved, it is well; and if he errs, he has erred from the path to Paradise. He who is humbled in this world [and honored in the Hereafter] is better than he who is honored in this world [and humbled in the Hereafter]."

Whoever prefers this world over the Hereafter, this world will tempt him and he will not attain the Hereafter. The angels marvelled at the goodness of his speech. Then he slept a sleep, and he was given wisdom. He woke up speaking it. [al-Muhadhdhab al-Bari' of Ibn Fahd: 4/454; Tarikh Dimashq: 17/85.]

Then Dawud was called after him, and he accepted it, but he did not stipulate what Luqman stipulated, so he fell into error more than once, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, pardoned him every time. Luqman used to support him with his wisdom. Dawud said to him: "Blessed are you, O Luqman. You were given wisdom and turned away from trial. Dawud was given the caliphate and was afflicted with calamity and temptation."

Al-Imam Abu Mansur ibn al-Jamshadhi narrated to us, in wording, saying: Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Yusuf narrated to me, from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad, from 'Abd Allah ibn Hashim, from Waki', from Muhammad ibn Hassan, from Khalid al-Rab'i, who said: Luqman was an Abyssinian slave and a carpenter. Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Fanjawayh informed us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn Malik al-Qati'i narrated to me, from 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal, from his father, from Aswad ibn 'Amir, from Hammad, from 'Ali ibn Yazid, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, that Luqman was a tailor.

﴿Be grateful to Allah﴾: meaning, "We said to him: be grateful to Allah."

﴿And whoever is grateful, he is only grateful for his own soul, and whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾.

Mujahid said: Luqman was a black slave with large lips and cracked feet. al-Awza'i narrated from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Harmalah, who said: A black man came to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, asking him. Sa'id said to him: "Do not grieve because you are black, for among the best of people were three from the blacks: Bilal, Mihja' the freedman of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and Luqman the wise. Luqman was a black Nubian from the blacks of Egypt, with thick lips."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when Luqman said to his son — his name was An'am — while he was advising him: "O my son, do not associate anything with Allah. Indeed, association is a great injustice."﴾ ﴿And We have enjoined upon man [regarding] his parents. His mother carried him, in weakness upon weakness﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: hardship upon hardship. al-Dahhak: weakness upon weakness. Qatadah: exertion upon exertion. Mujahid and Ibn Kaysan: difficulty upon difficulty.

﴿And his weaning is in two years﴾: its weaning, i.e. his removal from breastfeeding. It is narrated from Ya'qub: "wa-fisaluhu" (and his weaning).

﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents; to Me is the destination﴾. 'Abd Allah ibn Hamid al-Isfahani informed us, from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Balkhi, who said: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Balkhi informed me, from Nasir ibn Yahya, from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, concerning the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: "Give thanks to Me and to your parents." He said: Whoever prays the five prayers has given thanks to Allah, and whoever supplicates for his parents after the prayers has given thanks to his parents.

﴿And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them, but accompany them in this world with kindness﴾: good companionship; and its meaning is "with what is fair".

﴿And follow the way of those who turn back to Me﴾: take the path of Muhammad and his companions.

﴿Then to Me is your return, and I will inform you of what you used to do﴾. These two verses were revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and his mother, and the story has already passed.

﴿O my son, indeed it, if it be the weight of a mustard seed﴾. Some grammarians said: This pronoun refers to the sin and disobedience, meaning: indeed the disobedience, if it be. What supports this is the saying of Muqatil: An'am, the son of Luqman, said to his father: "O father, if I do a sin where no one sees me, how will Allah know it?" So he said to him: "O my son, indeed it, if it be..." Others said: this "ha'" is a supporting pronoun (imad), and it was made feminine because he took it to the grain, as in the saying of the poet:

"And he chokes on the word he has spread, as the spear's chest is choked with blood."

The "mithqal" may be read in the accusative or nominative: the accusative as the predicate of kana, and the nominative as its subject, and its meaning: "if there occurs" (in tam, complete usage), and then it has no predicate: ﴿then it would be in a rock﴾. Qatadah said: in a mountain. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a rock beneath the seven earths, and it is where the deeds of the wicked are recorded, and the greenness of the sky is from it. al-Suddi said: Allah created the earth upon a fish, which is the nun that Allah mentioned in the Qur'an: "Nun. By the pen" [68:1]. The fish is in the water, the water is on the back of a rock, the rock is on the back of an angel, and the angel is on a stone, and this is the rock that Luqman mentioned. It is neither in the heavens nor in the earth, and the rock is on the wind.

﴿Or in the heavens or in the earth — Allah will bring it forth. Indeed, Allah is Subtle [in extracting it], Acquainted [with its place].﴾ I saw in some books that Luqman (peace be upon him) said to his son: "O my son, indeed it, if it be the weight of a mustard seed..." to the end of the verse. He trembled from the awe of this word and died, and it was the last of his wisdom.

His saying: ﴿O my son, establish prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and bear patiently what befalls you. Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾: that is, the obligatory matters which Allah has commanded. Ibn 'Abbas said: the firm matters. Muqatil: the rightful matters.

﴿And do not turn your cheek [in contempt] toward people﴾. al-Nakha'i, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn Mahisn, Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "tusa'ir" with an alif.

Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Abu Habash informed me, Abu al-Qasim ibn al-Fadl said, Abu Zur'ah said: Nadr ibn 'Ali narrated to me, saying: my father informed me, from Mu'alla al-Warraq, from 'Asim al-Jahdari: "wa-la tusir khaddaka" with a damma on the ta' and a jazm on the sad, from "asara". The rest read "tusa'ir" from al-tasa'ir (the verb form). Ibn 'Abbas said: He means: do not be arrogant so that you belittle people and turn away from them with your face when they speak to you. Mujahid: it is the man who has a grudge between him and you, so you meet him and he turns his face away from you. 'Ikrimah: it is the one who, when greeted, twists his neck out of arrogance. al-Rabi' and Qatadah: do not belittle the poor; let the poor and the rich be equal in your sight. 'Ata': it is the one who twists his cheek.

'Abd Allah ibn Hamid informed us, from Hamid ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Salih, from 'Abd al-Samad, from Kharijah ibn Mus'ab, from al-Mughirah, from Ibrahim concerning His saying: "And do not turn your cheek toward people." He said: It is exaggerated speech (al-tashdiq fi al-kalam). al-Mu'arrikh said: do not frown at people's faces.

The origin of this word is inclination. It is said: "a man is asar" when his neck is inclined. Its plural is "sa'ar", and from it: al-sa'r, which is a disease that afflicts camels in their necks and heads until it twists their necks. The arrogant man who turns away from people in contempt for them is compared to that. A poet describing camels said:

"We brought them into the course of Suhayl, southerly, with the 'sa'r' of the desert, among the herd and the stragglers."

That is, inclined in the desert. Another said:

"And when the tyrant turned his cheek, we straightened him from his inclination, and he was made straight."

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾, meaning in conceit. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love everyone self-deluded and boastful﴾, in his walking, boasting over people.

'Abd Allah ibn Hamid al-Wazzan informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Shadhan, from Jaygawayh, from Salih ibn Muhammad, from Jarir ibn 'Abd al-Hamid, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from his father, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man went out swaggering in the Jahiliyyah, wearing a garment. So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, commanded the earth, and it seized him, and he continues sinking into it until the Day of Resurrection." [Musnad Ahmad: 2/222; Kanz al-'Ummal: 3/537, with variation in the hadith.]

﴿And be moderate in your walking﴾: be humble, and do not swagger, and let your walk be moderate, neither with conceit nor with haste.

Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn al-Husayn ibn Mihran al-Muqri' informed us in the year 381 [AH], saying: Abu al-'Abbas Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Surraj and Abu al-Wafa' al-Mu'ayyad ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Isa informed me, both saying: 'Abbas ibn Muhammad al-Duri said, from al-Walid ibn Salamah, judge of Jordan, from 'Umar ibn Sahban, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umran, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Haste in walking takes away the radiance of the believer." [183] [Kanz al-'Ummal: 15/412, no. 41620.]

﴿And lower your voice﴾, and reduce it: ﴿Indeed, the most disagreeable of voices is the voice of donkeys﴾. Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: the ugliest. Its beginning is a groan and its end is a sob; He commanded him to moderate his voice. 'Ikrimah and al-Hakam ibn 'Uyaynah said: the most intense. Ibn Zayd said: If raising the voice were good, He would not have assigned it to donkeys.

Abu Zakariyya Yahya ibn Isma'il al-Hari informed us, saying: Abu Hamid Ahmad ibn 'Abdun ibn 'Ammarah al-A'mash informed me, saying: Abu Hatim Muhammad ibn Idris al-Handhali informed me, from Yahya ibn Salih al-Wuhadhi, from Musa ibn A'yan, who said: I heard Sufyan say concerning the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: "Indeed, the most disagreeable of voices is the voice of donkeys": "The cry of every thing is glorification of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, except the donkey." It was also said: because it brays without benefit.

al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn Fanjawayh informed me, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Bishr, who said: Abu Bakr ibn Abi al-Khasib informed me, from 'Abd Allah ibn Jabir, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Walid al-Harrani, from 'Uthman ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from 'Anbasah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from Muhammad ibn Zadhan, from Umm Sa'd, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, dislikes three voices: the bray of the donkey, the bark of the dog, and the cry for war." [184]

Chapter on mention of some of the wisdom narrated from Luqman.

'Abd Allah ibn Hamid al-Wazzan al-Isfahani informed us, from Ahmad ibn Shadhan, from Jaygawayh ibn Muhammad [from Salih ibn Muhammad], from Ibrahim ibn Abi Yahya, from Muhammad ibn 'Ajlan, who said: Luqman said: "No wealth is like health, and no bounty is like a contented soul."

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Dinawari informed us, from 'Umar ibn Ahmad ibn al-Qasim al-Nahawandi, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Ghaffar al-Zarqani, from Abu Sukayn Zakariyya ibn Yahya ibn 'Umar ibn [Hafs (in the Isfahan copy: Hisn)], from his paternal uncle Abu Zajr ibn Hisn, from his grandfather Humayd ibn Minhab, who said: Tawus narrated to me, from Abu Hurayrah, who said:

A man passed by Luqman while people were gathered around him, and said: "Are you not the black slave who used to be a shepherd in such-and-such a place?" He said: "Yes." He said: "So what has brought you to what I see?" He said: "Truthfulness in speech, fulfilling trusts, and leaving what does not concern me."

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad informed me, saying: Abu al-Husayn Bakr ibn Malik al-Qati'i informed me, from 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal, from Ubayy, from Waki', who said: Abu al-Ashhab informed me, from Khalid al-Rab'i, who said: Luqman was an Abyssinian slave and a carpenter. His master said to him: "Slaughter a sheep for us." So he slaughtered a sheep for him. He said: "Bring me the best of its two morsels." So he brought him the tongue and the heart. He said: "Was there anything in it better than this?" He said: "No." He said: [Luqman] was silent about him, then said to him: "Slaughter a sheep for us," so he slaughtered a sheep, and he said: "Throw away its two worst morsels." So he threw away the tongue and the heart, and he said: "I ordered you to bring me the best of its two morsels, and you brought me the tongue and the heart; and I ordered you to throw away the worst of its two morsels, and you threw away the tongue and the heart?!" He said: "Because there is nothing better than them when they are good, and nothing worse than them when they are bad."

al-Husayn ibn Muhammad informed me, from Ahmad ibn Ja'far ibn Hamdan, from Yusuf ibn 'Abd Allah, from Musa ibn Isma'il, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Anas, that Luqman was with Dawud (peace be upon him) while he was weaving a coat of mail. Luqman kept marvelling at what he saw, and wanted to ask him, but his wisdom prevented him from asking. When he finished it, brought it and poured it out, he said: "What a fine coat of war this is!" Luqman said: "Indeed, among wise sayings is silence, and few are those who practise it."

[al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn Mahan informed me, from 'Ali ibn Muhammad al-Tanafasi (in the Isfahan copy: Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, from Ibn Shanbah, who said: 'Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Mahan narrated to us, from 'Ali ibn Muhammad al-Tanafasi)], who said: Abu Usamah and Waki' informed me, both saying: Sufyan informed us, from his father, from 'Ikrimah, who said: Luqman was among the least valued of his master's slaves. His master sent him with some slaves to an orchard of his to bring them some of its fruit. They came, having nothing with them, for they had eaten the fruit, and they blamed Luqman. Luqman said to his master: "The one of two faces is not trustworthy before Allah. Give me and them hot water to drink, then send us, and we will return." He did so, and they began to vomit that fruit, while Luqman vomited water. So his truthfulness and their lying became known.

He said: The first of his wisdom that was narrated: while he was with his master, he entered the privy and sat there a long time. Luqman called out to him: "Prolonged sitting over a need brings harm to the liver, produces hemorrhoids, and sends heat up to the head. So sit gently and rise gently." He said: So he came out and wrote his wisdom on the door of the latrine. [Tafsir al-Durr al-Manthur: 5/161, on the verse.]

He said: One day his master became drunk and bet some people that he would drink the water of a lake. When he sobered up, he realized what he had got into, so he summoned Luqman and said: "For such a thing I had chosen you." He said: "Bring out your chair and your jugs, then gather them." When they had gathered, he said: "On what did you bet?" They said: "That he would drink the water of this lake." He said: "It has sources. Block its sources from it." They said: "And how can we block its sources from it?" Luqman said: "And how can he drink it while it has sources?!"

al-Husayn ibn Muhammad informed me, from 'Ubayd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Shanbah, from 'Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Mahan, from 'Ali ibn Muhammad al-Tanafasi, who said: Abu al-Husayn al-'Ukli informed me [from 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal, from Dawud ibn 'Umar, from Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash, from 'Abd Allah ibn Dinar, that Luqman came back from a journey,] [In the Isfahan copy: from Abu al-Husayn al-'Ukli, from Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah al-Muzani, from his father, who said: Luqman said: "A father's beating of his child is like manure for the crop." al-Husayn ibn Muhammad informed me, saying: Abu Bakr ibn Malik narrated to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal narrated to us, saying: Dawud ibn 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash narrated to us, from 'Abd Allah ibn Dinar, that Luqman came back from a journey... the hadith.] and he met his servant on the road, and said: "What did my father do?" He said: "He died." He said: "Praise be to Allah, I have taken possession of my affair." He said: "What did my wife do?" He said: "She died." He said: "Renew my bedding." He said: "What did my sister do?" He said: "She died." He said: "She has covered my nakedness." He said: "What did my brother do?" He said: "He died." He said: "My back is broken."

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 31, verse 12–21 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad informed me, saying: Abu Bakr ibn Malik informed me, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal, from my father, from Sufyan, who said: It was said to Luqman: "Which of people is the most evil?" He said: "The one who does not care that people see him doing wrong." It was said to Luqman: "How ugly is your face!" He said: "Do you find fault with this on the engraving or on the engraver?"

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and has completed upon you His blessings?﴾

Nafiʿ, Shaybah, Abu Jaʿfar, Abu Raja' al-ʿUtaridi, Abu Mijlaz, Abu ʿAmr, al-Aʿraj, Ayyub and Hafs read "niʿamahu" (His blessings) in the plural with a pronoun suffix (idafah). Abu ʿUbayd, Abu Muʿadh al-Nahwi and Abu Hatim preferred this reading. The others read it in the singular with tanwin (niʿmatan), and its meaning is also plural. Its evidence is the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And if you count the blessings of Allah, you cannot enumerate them﴾ [Ibrahim: 34]. Mujahid and Sufyan said: they are "there is no god but Allah." Confirming this also is what Abu al-Qasim [al-Habibi] [sic in the original] informed me: that he saw in the codex of ʿAbd Allah "niʿmatahu" with the suffix and the singular, ﴿apparent and hidden﴾. They differed concerning it and said much.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: As for the apparent, it is religion and adornment; as for the hidden, it is what is concealed from the servants and known to Allah.

Muqatil: The apparent is the proportion of creation, provision and Islam; the hidden is the sins of the children of Adam that were concealed, so no one knew of them and they were not punished for them.

al-Dahhak: The apparent is beauty of form, height of stature and balance of limbs; the hidden is forgiveness.

al-Qurazi: The apparent is Muhammad (ﷺ), and the hidden is knowledge of Him.

Rabi': The apparent is by the limbs and the hidden is by the heart.

ʿAta' al-Khurasani: The apparent is the lightening of the laws, and the hidden is intercession.

Mujahid: The apparent is the manifestation of Islam and victory over enemies; the hidden is support with angels.

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Naysaburi informed us, saying: Abu al-Fadl Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn Mahmash informed us, saying: Abu Yahya Zakariyya ibn Yahya ibn al-Harb informed me, from Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Muhammad ibn Sabiq al-Kufi, who said: Abu Malik al-Jibni informed me, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, who said: I asked Ibn ʿAbbas about the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and has completed upon you His blessings, apparent and hidden﴾. He said: "This is from my memorized (reports) that I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what are these apparent and hidden blessings?' He said: 'As for the apparent, it is Islam, what is beautiful of your character, and what is bestowed upon you of provision. As for the hidden, it is what covers the evil of your deeds. O Ibn ʿAbbas, Allah the Exalted says: "I have made for the believer a third (of his reward) in the prayers of the believers over him after the cessation of his deeds, by which I expiate his sins; and I have made for him a third of his wealth so that he may expiate his sins by it; and I have concealed his evil deed which, if I were to reveal it to people, his family would cast him off, and others besides them."'"

Muhammad ibn ʿAli al-Tirmidhi said: The apparent blessing is ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed upon you My blessing﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], and the hidden is His saying: ﴿and I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3].

al-Harith ibn Asad al-Muhasibi [in the Isfahan copy: al-Harb ibn Asad al-Muharibi]: The apparent is the delight of this world, and the hidden is the delight of the Hereafter. ʿAmr ibn ʿUthman al-Sadafi: The apparent is the lightening of the laws, and the hidden is the multiplying of crafts.

It is said: The apparent is the reward, and the hidden is contentment. Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah: The apparent is following the Messenger, and the hidden is love for him. It is said: The apparent is the balancing of outward forms, and the hidden is the purifying of inner secrets. It is said: The apparent is clarification, its evidence being His saying: ﴿Allah makes clear to you lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisa': 176] and ﴿and He makes clear His signs to the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221]; and the hidden is adornment, as in His saying: ﴿and has made it beautiful in your hearts﴾ [al-Hujurat: 7]. It is said: The apparent is provision earned, and the hidden is provision ﴿from where he does not expect﴾.

It is said: The apparent is the entrance of food, and the hidden is the exit of harm. It is said: The apparent is the limbs, and the hidden is the interests. It is said: The apparent is creation, and the hidden is character. It is said: The apparent is bestowal of bounty, its evidence being His saying: ﴿those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7], and the hidden is teaching, as in His saying: ﴿and teaches you what you did not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 151]. It is said: The apparent is what is given and granted of blessings; it is said the hidden is what is folded and withheld of various kinds of trial. It is said: The apparent is the call, its evidence being His saying: ﴿and Allah calls to the abode of peace﴾ [Yunus: 25], and the hidden is guidance, its evidence being His saying: ﴿and guides whom He wills﴾ [Yunus: 25].

It is said: The apparent is support with angels, and the hidden is casting terror into the hearts of the disbelievers. It is said: The apparent is the detailing of acts of obedience, namely that He mentions your obedience one by one, praises you for it and rewards you for it, its evidence being His saying: ﴿the repentant﴾ [al-Tawbah: 112], and His saying: ﴿The believers have certainly succeeded﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 35] to the end of the verse. And the hidden is the summary of sins, for He called you to repentance from them by the name of faith without enumerating and detailing them, its evidence being His saying: ﴿And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you, O believers﴾ [al-Nur: 31]. It is said: The apparent is the sending down of rain and showers, and the hidden is the reviving of regions and cities.

It is said: The apparent is success in acts of worship, and the hidden is sincerity and protection from showing off. It is said: The apparent is the remembrance of the tongue, and the hidden is the remembrance of the heart. It is said: The apparent is recitation of the Qur'an, and the hidden is knowledge of it. It is said: The apparent is the light of day for activity and livelihood, and the hidden is the darkness of night for rest and repose. It is said: The apparent is speech, and the hidden is intellect. It is said: The apparent is His blessing upon you after you came out of your mother's womb, and the hidden is His blessing upon you while you were in your mother's womb.

It is said: The apparent is the manifest testimony, and the hidden is the prior happiness. It is said: The apparent is the variety of gifts, and the hidden is the forgiveness of sins. It is said: The apparent is the removal of burden and the raising of remembrance, and the hidden is the expansion of the breast.

It is said: The apparent is the opening of paths, and the hidden is the stripping of kingdoms from those who oppose You. It is said: The apparent is wealth and children, and the hidden is guidance and direction. It is said: The apparent is the sound word, and the hidden is confirmation and making upright. It is said: The apparent is what Allah expiates of sins through calamities and trials, and the hidden is what He pardons and does not hold you accountable for in this world and the Hereafter. It is said: The apparent is what lies between you and His creation of kinship and marriage ties, and the hidden is what lies between you and Him of nearness, secrets, and intimate conversation in the early hours. It is said: The apparent is height, its evidence being His saying: ﴿and you will be the superior ones﴾ [Al 'Imran: 139], and the hidden is nearness, its evidence being His saying: ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 11].

His saying: ﴿And among people is one who argues about Allah without knowledge or guidance or an illuminating Book﴾. It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith when he claimed that the angels are daughters of Allah. ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon."﴾

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Even though Satan invites them to the punishment of the Blaze?﴾ Al-Akhfash said: its wording is interrogative but its meaning is affirmative (taqrir). Abu ʿUbayda said: "law" here has an omitted answer; its implied sense is: ﴿Even though Satan invites them to the punishment of the Blaze?﴾, i.e., its requirements, so that they would follow him.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 31, verses 12–21 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾. It means reason, knowledge, acting upon it, and correctness in matters.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Yasar said: He was Luqman ibn Ba'ur ibn Bahur ibn Tarikh, and Tarikh is Azar. Wahb said: He was the son of Ayyub's sister. Muqatil said: It is mentioned that Luqman was the son of Ayyub's maternal aunt.

Al-Waqidi said: He was a judge among the Children of Israel. The scholars agreed that he was wise, but that he was not a prophet, except 'Ikrimah, who said: Luqman was a prophet. He stood alone in this view.

Abu Mansur al-Jamshadhi narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Yusuf narrated to me, from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from 'Abd Allah ibn Hashim, from Waki', from Isra'il, from Jabir, from 'Ikrimah, who said: Luqman was a prophet. Some of them said: Luqman was given the choice between prophethood and wisdom, and he chose wisdom.

'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar narrated, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Truly I say, Luqman was not a prophet, but he was a servant of Allah, abundant in reflection, good in certainty [in the source: "al-zann", opinion], who loved Allah, so Allah loved him, and He granted him wisdom by guarantee." [182] [Kanz al-'Ummal: 14/34.]

[It is narrated that at the beginning of his affair] Luqman was sleeping at midday when a call came to him: "O Luqman, would you like Allah to make you a khalifah (vicegerent) on earth, judging between people with truth?" He answered the voice, saying: "If my Lord gives me the choice, I will accept well-being and not accept trial. If He resolves upon me, then I hear and obey. For I know that if He does that to me, He will protect me and help me." The angels then said, in a voice they did not show, "Why, O Luqman?" He said: "Because the judge is in the most difficult and turbid of positions; injustice overtakes him from every place. If he is saved, it is well; and if he errs, he has erred from the path to Paradise. He who is humbled in this world [and honored in the Hereafter] is better than he who is honored in this world [and humbled in the Hereafter]."

Whoever prefers this world over the Hereafter, this world will tempt him and he will not attain the Hereafter. The angels marvelled at the goodness of his speech. Then he slept a sleep, and he was given wisdom. He woke up speaking it. [al-Muhadhdhab al-Bari' of Ibn Fahd: 4/454; Tarikh Dimashq: 17/85.]

Then Dawud was called after him, and he accepted it, but he did not stipulate what Luqman stipulated, so he fell into error more than once, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, pardoned him every time. Luqman used to support him with his wisdom. Dawud said to him: "Blessed are you, O Luqman. You were given wisdom and turned away from trial. Dawud was given the caliphate and was afflicted with calamity and temptation."

Al-Imam Abu Mansur ibn al-Jamshadhi narrated to us, in wording, saying: Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Yusuf narrated to me, from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad, from 'Abd Allah ibn Hashim, from Waki', from Muhammad ibn Hassan, from Khalid al-Rab'i, who said: Luqman was an Abyssinian slave and a carpenter. Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Fanjawayh informed us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn Malik al-Qati'i narrated to me, from 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal, from his father, from Aswad ibn 'Amir, from Hammad, from 'Ali ibn Yazid, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, that Luqman was a tailor.

﴿Be grateful to Allah﴾: meaning, "We said to him: be grateful to Allah."

﴿And whoever is grateful, he is only grateful for his own soul, and whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾.

Mujahid said: Luqman was a black slave with large lips and cracked feet. al-Awza'i narrated from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Harmalah, who said: A black man came to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, asking him. Sa'id said to him: "Do not grieve because you are black, for among the best of people were three from the blacks: Bilal, Mihja' the freedman of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and Luqman the wise. Luqman was a black Nubian from the blacks of Egypt, with thick lips."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when Luqman said to his son — his name was An'am — while he was advising him: "O my son, do not associate anything with Allah. Indeed, association is a great injustice."﴾ ﴿And We have enjoined upon man [regarding] his parents. His mother carried him, in weakness upon weakness﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: hardship upon hardship. al-Dahhak: weakness upon weakness. Qatadah: exertion upon exertion. Mujahid and Ibn Kaysan: difficulty upon difficulty.

﴿And his weaning is in two years﴾: its weaning, i.e. his removal from breastfeeding. It is narrated from Ya'qub: "wa-fisaluhu" (and his weaning).

﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents; to Me is the destination﴾. 'Abd Allah ibn Hamid al-Isfahani informed us, from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Balkhi, who said: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Balkhi informed me, from Nasir ibn Yahya, from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, concerning the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: "Give thanks to Me and to your parents." He said: Whoever prays the five prayers has given thanks to Allah, and whoever supplicates for his parents after the prayers has given thanks to his parents.

﴿And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them, but accompany them in this world with kindness﴾: good companionship; and its meaning is "with what is fair".

﴿And follow the way of those who turn back to Me﴾: take the path of Muhammad and his companions.

﴿Then to Me is your return, and I will inform you of what you used to do﴾. These two verses were revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and his mother, and the story has already passed.

﴿O my son, indeed it, if it be the weight of a mustard seed﴾. Some grammarians said: This pronoun refers to the sin and disobedience, meaning: indeed the disobedience, if it be. What supports this is the saying of Muqatil: An'am, the son of Luqman, said to his father: "O father, if I do a sin where no one sees me, how will Allah know it?" So he said to him: "O my son, indeed it, if it be..." Others said: this "ha'" is a supporting pronoun (imad), and it was made feminine because he took it to the grain, as in the saying of the poet:

"And he chokes on the word he has spread, as the spear's chest is choked with blood."

The "mithqal" may be read in the accusative or nominative: the accusative as the predicate of kana, and the nominative as its subject, and its meaning: "if there occurs" (in tam, complete usage), and then it has no predicate: ﴿then it would be in a rock﴾. Qatadah said: in a mountain. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a rock beneath the seven earths, and it is where the deeds of the wicked are recorded, and the greenness of the sky is from it. al-Suddi said: Allah created the earth upon a fish, which is the nun that Allah mentioned in the Qur'an: "Nun. By the pen" [68:1]. The fish is in the water, the water is on the back of a rock, the rock is on the back of an angel, and the angel is on a stone, and this is the rock that Luqman mentioned. It is neither in the heavens nor in the earth, and the rock is on the wind.

﴿Or in the heavens or in the earth — Allah will bring it forth. Indeed, Allah is Subtle [in extracting it], Acquainted [with its place].﴾ I saw in some books that Luqman (peace be upon him) said to his son: "O my son, indeed it, if it be the weight of a mustard seed..." to the end of the verse. He trembled from the awe of this word and died, and it was the last of his wisdom.

His saying: ﴿O my son, establish prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and bear patiently what befalls you. Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾: that is, the obligatory matters which Allah has commanded. Ibn 'Abbas said: the firm matters. Muqatil: the rightful matters.

﴿And do not turn your cheek [in contempt] toward people﴾. al-Nakha'i, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn Mahisn, Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "tusa'ir" with an alif.

Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Abu Habash informed me, Abu al-Qasim ibn al-Fadl said, Abu Zur'ah said: Nadr ibn 'Ali narrated to me, saying: my father informed me, from Mu'alla al-Warraq, from 'Asim al-Jahdari: "wa-la tusir khaddaka" with a damma on the ta' and a jazm on the sad, from "asara". The rest read "tusa'ir" from al-tasa'ir (the verb form). Ibn 'Abbas said: He means: do not be arrogant so that you belittle people and turn away from them with your face when they speak to you. Mujahid: it is the man who has a grudge between him and you, so you meet him and he turns his face away from you. 'Ikrimah: it is the one who, when greeted, twists his neck out of arrogance. al-Rabi' and Qatadah: do not belittle the poor; let the poor and the rich be equal in your sight. 'Ata': it is the one who twists his cheek.

'Abd Allah ibn Hamid informed us, from Hamid ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Salih, from 'Abd al-Samad, from Kharijah ibn Mus'ab, from al-Mughirah, from Ibrahim concerning His saying: "And do not turn your cheek toward people." He said: It is exaggerated speech (al-tashdiq fi al-kalam). al-Mu'arrikh said: do not frown at people's faces.

The origin of this word is inclination. It is said: "a man is asar" when his neck is inclined. Its plural is "sa'ar", and from it: al-sa'r, which is a disease that afflicts camels in their necks and heads until it twists their necks. The arrogant man who turns away from people in contempt for them is compared to that. A poet describing camels said:

"We brought them into the course of Suhayl, southerly, with the 'sa'r' of the desert, among the herd and the stragglers."

That is, inclined in the desert. Another said:

"And when the tyrant turned his cheek, we straightened him from his inclination, and he was made straight."

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾, meaning in conceit. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love everyone self-deluded and boastful﴾, in his walking, boasting over people.

'Abd Allah ibn Hamid al-Wazzan informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Shadhan, from Jaygawayh, from Salih ibn Muhammad, from Jarir ibn 'Abd al-Hamid, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from his father, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man went out swaggering in the Jahiliyyah, wearing a garment. So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, commanded the earth, and it seized him, and he continues sinking into it until the Day of Resurrection." [Musnad Ahmad: 2/222; Kanz al-'Ummal: 3/537, with variation in the hadith.]

﴿And be moderate in your walking﴾: be humble, and do not swagger, and let your walk be moderate, neither with conceit nor with haste.

Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn al-Husayn ibn Mihran al-Muqri' informed us in the year 381 [AH], saying: Abu al-'Abbas Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Surraj and Abu al-Wafa' al-Mu'ayyad ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Isa informed me, both saying: 'Abbas ibn Muhammad al-Duri said, from al-Walid ibn Salamah, judge of Jordan, from 'Umar ibn Sahban, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umran, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Haste in walking takes away the radiance of the believer." [183] [Kanz al-'Ummal: 15/412, no. 41620.]

﴿And lower your voice﴾, and reduce it: ﴿Indeed, the most disagreeable of voices is the voice of donkeys﴾. Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: the ugliest. Its beginning is a groan and its end is a sob; He commanded him to moderate his voice. 'Ikrimah and al-Hakam ibn 'Uyaynah said: the most intense. Ibn Zayd said: If raising the voice were good, He would not have assigned it to donkeys.

Abu Zakariyya Yahya ibn Isma'il al-Hari informed us, saying: Abu Hamid Ahmad ibn 'Abdun ibn 'Ammarah al-A'mash informed me, saying: Abu Hatim Muhammad ibn Idris al-Handhali informed me, from Yahya ibn Salih al-Wuhadhi, from Musa ibn A'yan, who said: I heard Sufyan say concerning the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: "Indeed, the most disagreeable of voices is the voice of donkeys": "The cry of every thing is glorification of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, except the donkey." It was also said: because it brays without benefit.

al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn Fanjawayh informed me, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Bishr, who said: Abu Bakr ibn Abi al-Khasib informed me, from 'Abd Allah ibn Jabir, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Walid al-Harrani, from 'Uthman ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from 'Anbasah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from Muhammad ibn Zadhan, from Umm Sa'd, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, dislikes three voices: the bray of the donkey, the bark of the dog, and the cry for war." [184]

Chapter on mention of some of the wisdom narrated from Luqman.

'Abd Allah ibn Hamid al-Wazzan al-Isfahani informed us, from Ahmad ibn Shadhan, from Jaygawayh ibn Muhammad [from Salih ibn Muhammad], from Ibrahim ibn Abi Yahya, from Muhammad ibn 'Ajlan, who said: Luqman said: "No wealth is like health, and no bounty is like a contented soul."

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Dinawari informed us, from 'Umar ibn Ahmad ibn al-Qasim al-Nahawandi, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Ghaffar al-Zarqani, from Abu Sukayn Zakariyya ibn Yahya ibn 'Umar ibn [Hafs (in the Isfahan copy: Hisn)], from his paternal uncle Abu Zajr ibn Hisn, from his grandfather Humayd ibn Minhab, who said: Tawus narrated to me, from Abu Hurayrah, who said:

A man passed by Luqman while people were gathered around him, and said: "Are you not the black slave who used to be a shepherd in such-and-such a place?" He said: "Yes." He said: "So what has brought you to what I see?" He said: "Truthfulness in speech, fulfilling trusts, and leaving what does not concern me."

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad informed me, saying: Abu al-Husayn Bakr ibn Malik al-Qati'i informed me, from 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal, from Ubayy, from Waki', who said: Abu al-Ashhab informed me, from Khalid al-Rab'i, who said: Luqman was an Abyssinian slave and a carpenter. His master said to him: "Slaughter a sheep for us." So he slaughtered a sheep for him. He said: "Bring me the best of its two morsels." So he brought him the tongue and the heart. He said: "Was there anything in it better than this?" He said: "No." He said: [Luqman] was silent about him, then said to him: "Slaughter a sheep for us," so he slaughtered a sheep, and he said: "Throw away its two worst morsels." So he threw away the tongue and the heart, and he said: "I ordered you to bring me the best of its two morsels, and you brought me the tongue and the heart; and I ordered you to throw away the worst of its two morsels, and you threw away the tongue and the heart?!" He said: "Because there is nothing better than them when they are good, and nothing worse than them when they are bad."

al-Husayn ibn Muhammad informed me, from Ahmad ibn Ja'far ibn Hamdan, from Yusuf ibn 'Abd Allah, from Musa ibn Isma'il, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Anas, that Luqman was with Dawud (peace be upon him) while he was weaving a coat of mail. Luqman kept marvelling at what he saw, and wanted to ask him, but his wisdom prevented him from asking. When he finished it, brought it and poured it out, he said: "What a fine coat of war this is!" Luqman said: "Indeed, among wise sayings is silence, and few are those who practise it."
